questions.q: The basic communication chain for train operations is:
options: Operations Control Centre (OCC) ↔ Station ↔ Train ↔ Field staff
Train ↔ passengers ↔ station ↔ Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Operations run on one chain — Operations Control Centre (OCC), station, train and field staff — so every message reaches the level that can act on it.

questions.q: Operational radio and telephone conversations are preferably made on channels that are:
options: Recorded, because recordings are evidence of correct working
questions.explain: Recorded channels protect everyone: after an incident, the recording shows exactly what was said and ordered.

questions.q: Which call gets priority over all routine radio traffic?
options: A defect report for the next day
questions.explain: Emergency calls override everything. All other users must keep the channel clear until the emergency is handled.

questions.q: The FIRST thing you do when starting any safety-critical message is:
options: Ask the receiver to guess your identity
End with your name only if asked
State who you are, your location/designation, and who you are calling
questions.explain: Identify first, every time. The receiver must know who is speaking and from where before acting on a message.

questions.q: A good safety-critical message contains:
options: One instruction per message, in short standard phrases
Extra background stories to make it interesting
questions.explain: One instruction per message, in standard words. Packing many instructions together creates confusion and wrong actions.

questions.q: In the phonetic alphabet, the letter 'M' is spoken as:
questions.explain: M = Mike in the NATO phonetic alphabet, used so letters are not confused in poor audio.

questions.q: In the phonetic alphabet, 'S' and 'T' are spoken as:
questions.explain: S = Sierra and T = Tango. Standard words remove sound-alike confusion on noisy channels.

questions.q: The phonetic words for 'P' and 'R' are:
questions.explain: P = Papa and R = Romeo in the prescribed phonetic alphabet.

questions.q: Critical numbers such as train IDs, speeds and times should be spoken:
options: In round figures to save time
questions.explain: 'One-five' cannot be confused with 'five-zero'. Digit-by-digit speaking protects critical numbers in noise.

questions.q: Times in operational communication are given in:
questions.explain: 24-hour format removes AM/PM confusion — 14:05 can only mean one time of day.

questions.q: Read-back means the receiver:
options: Reads the next instruction in advance
Reads the message from a notebook
Repeats the instruction back so the sender can confirm it
Records the call on his phone
questions.explain: Read-back closes the loop: the sender hears his own order repeated and can catch any error before it is acted on.

questions.q: After a correct read-back, the sender must:
questions.explain: The loop is: message → read-back → sender confirms 'correct'. Without confirmation the exchange is incomplete.

questions.q: An instruction that has NOT been acknowledged must be treated as:
questions.explain: An unacknowledged instruction is treated as not received. Silence on a radio proves nothing.

questions.q: Closing the loop of an instruction means:
options: Reporting completion back, e.g. 'Task complete, section clear'
Asking someone else to finish it
questions.explain: Every instruction ends with a completion report. An open-ended instruction leaves the sender guessing about safety.

questions.q: A driver receives an instruction that seems unsafe. The correct action is:
options: Ask a passenger what to do
Challenge it politely through procedure and ask for clarification
questions.explain: Silence is not consent in safety communication. An unclear or unsafe instruction must be challenged through procedure.

questions.q: During normal operations, routine reports (departures, arrivals, defects) are made:
options: At defined points, in standard format
Only at the end of the shift
questions.explain: Normal protocol = routine reports at defined points in a standard format, so Operations Control Centre (OCC) always has a predictable picture.

questions.q: When an abnormal situation develops, the communication protocol changes first by:
options: Declaring 'Emergency' upfront and taking emergency priority
Waiting for the next routine report point
questions.explain: State 'Emergency' upfront. That one word changes the priority of the call and the attention of everyone listening.

questions.q: The structured emergency brief should contain, in order of usefulness:
options: What, Where, When, Who/What is involved, Casualties, Action taken, Help needed
questions.explain: The What–Where–When–Who–Casualties–Action–Help format gives Operations Control Centre (OCC) a complete picture in one short message.

questions.q: After the first emergency message, the site should:
options: Let passengers update Operations Control Centre (OCC)
questions.explain: Emergencies are reported continuously, not once. Operations Control Centre (OCC) plans on fresh information until the emergency is stood down.

questions.q: A station controller gets a garbled message where the train number is unclear. He should:
options: Act on the part he heard
Ask for the message to be repeated and the number read back digit by digit
questions.explain: Never act on a guessed number. Ask for repetition — a wrong train number can send help or authority to the wrong train.

questions.q: Operations Control Centre (OCC) instructs a driver: 'Hold at the next station.' The driver repeats a different station name in read-back. Operations Control Centre (OCC) must:
options: Cancel all movements for the day
Let it pass to save time
Correct the read-back immediately and get a fresh, correct read-back
questions.explain: A wrong read-back is exactly what the system exists to catch. Correct it on the radio, not on the track.

questions.q: Two stations try to transmit at the same time during an emergency. Correct channel discipline is:
options: Routine users keep the channel clear for the emergency traffic
The senior officer's station talks over everyone
questions.explain: In an emergency the channel belongs to the emergency. Routine traffic waits and keeps the channel clear.

questions.q: A train operator must pass a letter-based equipment ID in poor audio conditions. He should use:
options: The phonetic alphabet for each letter
questions.explain: Phonetic words are designed for poor audio — each letter gets a unique, unmistakable word.

questions.q: Which is an example of clear and concise safety communication?
options: 'There is some issue somewhere, do something'
'Operations Control Centre (OCC), Train 204 at Station X — door fault, holding, request instructions'
A long story about the shift so far
questions.explain: Identity + train + location + problem + request, in one short message. Vague messages waste the minutes that matter.

questions.q: A field staff member completes a protection task but does not report it, assuming Operations Control Centre (OCC) 'will know'. This is wrong because:
options: An unreported task leaves the instruction open and Operations Control Centre (OCC) cannot safely plan the next movement
OCC can see everything on Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) anyway
questions.explain: Close the loop. Until completion is reported, Operations Control Centre (OCC) must treat the section as not confirmed clear.

questions.q: During degraded working, Operations Control Centre (OCC) gives a verbal authority. The receiver's read-back is correct but the sender does not confirm. The receiver should:
options: Treat the authority as incomplete and seek the sender's confirmation
questions.explain: Message, read-back and confirmation are one package. Without the sender's 'correct', the loop is not closed.

questions.q: Passing operational messages through a chain of people by word of mouth is risky mainly because:
options: Each retelling can distort the message — the 'telephone game' effect
questions.explain: Like the children's telephone game, messages distort at every pass. Direct, confirmed communication prevents that.

questions.q: A station receives an Operations Control Centre (OCC) instruction meant for another station with a similar name. The station should:
options: Forward it by guessing the right station
Act on it to be helpful
Clarify with Operations Control Centre (OCC) immediately that the message may be mis-addressed
questions.explain: Similar names are a known trap. Clarify the addressee before anyone acts — acting on another station's instruction can be dangerous.

questions.q: Which habit best protects a controller during a busy, noisy shift?
options: Giving several instructions in one breath
Using standard phrases, one instruction per message, with read-back
questions.explain: Under pressure, standard short phrases with read-back are faster in effect — they prevent the errors that cost real time.

questions.q: An emergency call format/address is prescribed mainly so that:
options: The emergency gets instant attention and priority on the channel
questions.explain: The prescribed emergency format is a signal everyone recognises instantly — it buys attention in the first second.

questions.q: A driver is told a speed restriction value over a crackling radio. The safest practice is:
options: Have the value spoken digit by digit and read it back
questions.explain: Critical values are spoken digit by digit and read back. Memory and guesswork have no place with safety numbers.

questions.q: After an incident is over, why do recordings of operational calls matter?
options: They are used for entertainment in training only
They are evidence of what was ordered and acknowledged, for the enquiry
They replace the written report fully
questions.explain: Speak as if the enquiry will listen — because it may. Recordings prove the exact words, times and acknowledgements.

questions.q: In normal running, a train reports a minor defect that does not affect safety. The correct protocol is:
options: Report it at the defined point in standard format and continue as instructed
Stop the train wherever it is
questions.explain: Not everything is an emergency. Routine defects follow normal protocol — defined points, standard format, Operations Control Centre (OCC) decides the action.

questions.q: The phrase 'silence is not consent' in safety communication means:
options: If you do not understand or do not agree, you must speak up — quietness is never taken as agreement
questions.explain: In safety work, not objecting is never treated as agreeing. Doubt must be voiced through procedure.

questions.q: A controller must pass the ID 'B7' over the radio. The correct way is:
options: Spell it in the local language
'Bravo seven' — letter in phonetic form, number spoken clearly
questions.explain: Letters go phonetic (B = Bravo) and numbers are spoken clearly, so 'B7' cannot be heard as 'D7' or 'P7'.

questions.q: Over the radio you did not understand an instruction. The correct standard phrase to ask for it again is:
options: 'Say again' — asking the sender to transmit the message once more
You stay silent and guess the meaning
questions.explain: Standard phraseology removes guesswork: 'Say again' is the recognised request for retransmission. Guessing a safety instruction is never an option.

questions.q: In radio discipline, the word 'Roger' spoken by a receiver means:
options: I will obey after some time
I have received and understood your message
questions.explain: 'Roger' closes the receiving half of the loop: received and understood. Where the instruction also needs action, read-back of the actual content is still the stronger proof.

questions.q: The Operations Control Centre (OCC) needs to give one instruction — a speed restriction — to every train in an area at the same time. The efficient radio method is:
options: Calling each train one by one over the next hour
A group (all-call) broadcast to all trains in that area, with each train acknowledging in turn
Putting up a notice at the depot
Waiting till trains reach their terminals
questions.explain: A group call reaches everyone together, and ordered acknowledgements confirm nobody missed it. One-by-one calling leaves early trains uninformed for too long.

questions.q: At shift change, the outgoing controller's communication duty to the incoming controller is:
options: A proper handover — verbal briefing plus the written log — covering live incidents, restrictions, failed equipment and pending actions
Leaving a note only if something exploded
questions.explain: More incidents grow out of poor handovers than out of machines. The incoming controller must start with the same picture the outgoing one ended with — spoken and written.

questions.q: A driver enters a known radio dead zone (a short stretch with no coverage) and must contact the Operations Control Centre (OCC). The correct practice is:
options: Keep shouting into the radio till someone answers
Use the fixed telephone at the next station or another prescribed channel rather than relying on the dead-zone radio, and inform the Operations Control Centre (OCC) at the first working contact point
Stop the train in the dead zone and wait
Send a message through a passenger's phone
questions.explain: Dead zones are known in advance, so the procedure is planned: communicate from where communication exists. Unplanned silence is what creates danger.
